strengths: Clear and verifiable novelty: the paper presents the first extension of the functional maps framework from surfaces to volumetric (tetrahedral) meshes, an open problem explicitly identified in the literature ([91, §8.2]), and the related work section carefully documents the absence of prior spectral approaches to volume mapping.

Technically sound foundation: the extension is grounded in established theory — the n-dimensional cotangent LBO, the linear-independence of boundary traces of eigenfunctions under Neumann conditions ([51, 117]) supporting the spectral extrapolation of interior coordinates, and Weyl's-law corrections (Appendix B) for comparing 2D vs 3D spectra. Appendices C–D provide empirical studies (geodesic distortion, boundary-trace reconstruction) that justify the key assumptions.

Strong empirical validation across multiple tasks: volumetric shape matching with ground truth (Fig. 4), connectivity transfer quantified by percentage of flipped tetrahedra at varying basis sizes (Tab. 1, Fig. 13), bootstrapping of untangling algorithms — resolving 85% of the 1405 documented failure cases of a state-of-the-art pipeline (Fig. 6) — segmentation transfer to medical brain shapes (Fig. 8), solid texturing, and improved surface shape matching on SHREC'19/'20, TOPKIDS, and VOL (Tab. 2, Fig. 15).

Honest treatment of limitations: the authors explicitly acknowledge that full injectivity requires prohibitively large spectra, that the accuracy gain in shape matching is largely explained by the extra internal vertices (slowdown closely tracking vertex ratio), and that tetrahedralization noise can degrade results (SHREC'20 with LBO basis). This transparency strengthens the credibility of the claims.
Good reproducibility posture: pseudocode for all three algorithms (Appendix I), precise hyperparameter settings (basis sizes, ZoomOut schedule), and released reference code.

High practical significance: connectivity transfer, segmentation transfer, and improved warm-starting of volumetric untangling pipelines address genuinely open problems relevant to medical imaging, meshing, and fabrication.
weaknesses: Conceptual contribution is an adaptation rather than a new method: the core machinery (LBO eigenbasis, functional map estimation, ZoomOut refinement) is imported from the surface setting, and the volumetric LBO discretization is standard. The most novel algorithmic pieces (boundary-trace extrapolation, Eq. 8-9) are elegant but technically simple; a deeper theoretical analysis of volumetric functional maps (acknowledged as future work) is absent.

Shape matching evaluation is limited to classical spectral baselines (FMaps, ZoomOut, Orthoprods). The claim that volumetric maps 'consistently outperform surface-only spectral methods' holds within this restricted family; comparisons against modern learning-based matchers (e.g., GeFM, deep functional maps variants) or other volumetric approaches are absent, so the broader significance of the accuracy gain is hard to gauge. Notably, on SHREC'20 the surface approach is actually more accurate for two of the three bases (Tab. 2).

The medical application (Sec. 5.3) is only a qualitative demonstration on two brain shapes plus a template; no quantitative segmentation-transfer metric or comparison against existing volumetric registration methods (e.g., LDDMM) is provided, weakening the medical-applicability claims in the abstract and introduction.

Computational cost is significant: ~1127s for the largest basis and connectivity transfer requiring 25% of the spectrum for full injectivity makes the method expensive on large meshes; the paper leaves this open rather than proposing a mitigation.

The volumetric accuracy advantage in Sec. 5.4 is partly an artifact of mesh resolution: the slowdown correlates with the vertex ratio (1.4×–2.5×), so a fairer comparison would also include surface methods with comparable vertex counts, which is not reported.

Some experiments rest on a modest dataset (40 pairs from Su et al. [113] with shared connectivity, hence intrinsically easy for matching — the authors themselves note the AGE is 10^-6 scale), and the qualitative claims in Sec. 5.1 are not always backed by statistical significance testing.

strengths: The paper presents the first extension of the functional maps framework to volumetric (tetrahedral) data, filling a genuine gap identified in the related work (piece-wise volume mapping is mature, spectral volume mapping is absent). This is a clear and well-motivated original contribution.

The core technical idea is sound and well-supported: the volumetric LBO eigenbasis provides a discretization-agnostic function space, and the key observation that boundary traces of volumetric eigenfunctions are linearly independent (backed by control theory results [51, 117] and an empirical study in Appendix D) enables both connectivity transfer from surface correspondences and spectral extrapolation of interior coordinates.

The empirical validation is broad: quantitative evaluation with ground-truth correspondences on 40 tetrahedral pairs (Fig. 4, Tab. 3), connectivity transfer quantified by flipped-cell ratios vs. basis size (Tab. 1, Fig. 13), a large-scale untangling bootstrapping experiment resolving 85% of 1405 failures from Nigolian et al. [83], and surface shape matching on four datasets (VOL, SHREC'19, SHREC'20, TOPKIDS) across three bases (Tab. 2, Fig. 15).

The appendices contain genuinely useful analysis, e.g., correcting the spectral comparison for the dimension-dependent Weyl's law (Appendix B), empirical verification that volumetric geodesic distortion is comparable to surface distortion (Appendix C), and honest discussion of basis-choice effects (Appendix H, Fig. 16).

Practical applications (solid texturing, segmentation transfer to medical scans, connectivity transfer for fabrication/meshing) demonstrate usefulness beyond shape matching, and code plus pseudocode support reproducibility.
The limitations section is candid: injectivity is not guaranteed for fixed spectrum size, computational overhead is intrinsic, and theoretical invariance analysis is left to future work.
weaknesses: The claim of 'consistently outperforming surface-only spectral methods' is overstated: on SHREC'20 with LBO and Orthoprods bases, the surface approach achieves lower AGE (e.g., 1.82e-1 vs. 2.72e-1 with LBO), and the volumetric advantage only materializes with specific bases (CMH), as the authors themselves concede. Success rates of 22.5% on VOL and 14.8% on SHREC'20 (LBO) indicate high variance.

There is no quantitative comparison against alternative volumetric mapping approaches (e.g., LDDMM-style registration, Su et al. [113], Du et al. [28], Garanzha et al. [36]) on map accuracy for the main matching task; the untangling experiment uses prior methods only as a downstream stage, so the practical accuracy/robustness positioning relative to the piece-wise volume mapping literature remains qualitative.

The main validation dataset (VOL) is acknowledged by the authors to be easy (watertight, shared connectivity, AGE ~1e-6), and the other datasets are derived via fTetWild tetrahedralization, whose topological artifacts the authors show can dominate results; the evaluation breadth is therefore narrower than the framing suggests.
Segmentation transfer and solid texturing are demonstrated only qualitatively on one or two shapes (Figs. 5 and 8), with no quantitative or user-facing evaluation of these applications.

Computational overhead is significant and resolution-coupled (e.g., 1127s for large bases; slowdowns up to 2.5x), and full injectivity may require 25% of the spectrum, which the authors admit can be computationally prohibitive.

Presentation issues: several typos ('voulmetric', 'existing approach are limited'), placeholder/broken URLs in the text and references ('https://Here', 'anonymous'), and some results are described as 'educated guesses' rather than established claims (e.g., why CMH regularizes SHREC'20).

strengths: Clear and well-motivated novelty: the paper extends the functional maps framework to volumetric (tetrahedral) domains for the first time, addressing a genuine gap the related-work section documents carefully (no prior spectral approach to volume mapping; piece-wise volume maps are known to be fragile).

The method is technically sound and not a trivial port: key obstacles of the volumetric setting are explicitly identified and addressed, e.g., reliance on the linear independence of boundary traces of eigenfunctions under Neumann conditions (cited to control theory results and analyzed empirically in Appendix D), Neumann boundary conditions to avoid degenerate surface eigenfunctions, and a Weyl-law-based rescaling for comparing 2D vs. 3D spectra (Appendix B).

Comprehensive validation: quantitative results on a volumetric ground-truth dataset (Su et al., 40 pairs), plus tetrahedralized versions of SHREC'19, SHREC'20, and TOPKIDS; multiple bases (LBO, CMH, Orthoprods) and pipelines (FMaps, ZoomOut, ZoomOut Fast) are compared, with honest reporting of where the volumetric approach does not win (e.g., SHREC'20 with LBO/Orthoprods).

Strong practical impact demonstrated beyond benchmark numbers: connectivity transfer is bootstrapped into a state-of-the-art untangling pipeline and resolves 85% of the 1405 documented failure cases of Garanzha et al., which is a significant, verifiable improvement to a known open problem; additional applications (solid texturing, segmentation transfer to medical data, mesh connectivity transfer) show real utility.

Honest limitation discussion (spectrum size needed for full injectivity, computational overhead correlated with added vertices, dataset tetrahedralization challenges) and thorough supporting appendices (spectral invariance studies, isometry distortion analysis, pseudocode) make the work reproducible; code is released.
Extra contributions to the community: volumetric extensions of standard evaluation metrics and an analysis of why/when volume information helps surface matching, which will inform follow-up work.
weaknesses: The headline claim that volumetric maps 'consistently outperform' surface-only methods is only partially supported: Table 2 shows consistent wins on SHREC'19 and TOPKIDS, but on the volumetric ground-truth dataset VOL the surface variant wins with LBO and CMH (volumetric wins only with Orthoprods at 60% success rate), and on SHREC'20 the LBO and Orthoprods volumetric variants are worse than surface, with the win coming only after switching to CMH. The consistency claim should be more carefully qualified.

Accuracy gains are often modest and heavily dependent on basis choice and tetrahedralization quality; the dependence on fTetWild output quality (topological artifacts, discarded meshes in SHREC'20) introduces a confound that the authors acknowledge but do not fully quantify.

Computational cost is significant: slowdowns of roughly 1.9x-2.5x plus basis computation times up to ~1127 s, and full injectivity of connectivity transfer may require a prohibitively large spectrum; this limits practicality on large meshes, as the authors themselves note.

The connectivity transfer and extrapolation pipelines presuppose a known surface correspondence pi, so the evaluation of volumetric matching quality is confined to a small dataset (40 pairs, largely watertight with shared connectivity) where the authors themselves concede shape matching is 'not really challenging'; the stress-tested datasets are surface datasets tetrahedralized post hoc rather than genuinely volumetric matching problems.

Some qualitative results (Fig. 8 segmentation transfer is shown on only two brains; Fig. 6 untangling rescue) lack quantitative aggregate metrics for the segmentation application, and there are minor presentation issues (typos such as 'voulmetric', informal phrasing like 'we guess', 'educatively guess') that should be cleaned up.

The theoretical treatment remains empirical: no theorem is established for when volumetric functional maps are superior to surface maps, and the invariance properties are verified by experiment rather than proven; the authors appropriately flag this as future work.
